questions.questionText: Which interface is the root of the Java Collections Framework?
questions.hint: Map is not part of this hierarchy.
questions.explanation: The Collection interface is the root of the collections hierarchy. List, Set, and Queue extend Collection. Map is separate.

questions.hint: Sets do not allow duplicates by definition.
questions.explanation: ArrayList (and all List implementations) allows duplicate elements. Set implementations (HashSet, TreeSet) do not allow duplicates.

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of ArrayList.get(index)?
questions.hint: ArrayList uses an internal array for storage.
questions.explanation: ArrayList stores elements in a contiguous array, so accessing by index is O(1) constant time.

questions.questionText: Which collection guarantees FIFO (First-In, First-Out) order?
questions.hint: A queue processes elements in the order they arrive.
questions.explanation: LinkedList implements the Queue interface and provides FIFO ordering. PriorityQueue orders by priority, not insertion order.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between HashMap and TreeMap?
options: HashMap is sorted; TreeMap is not
TreeMap maintains sorted key order; HashMap does not guarantee order
HashMap uses linked lists; TreeMap uses arrays
questions.hint: One uses a hash table, the other uses a red-black tree.
questions.explanation: TreeMap sorts entries by natural key order (or a Comparator). HashMap does not guarantee any order. TreeMap operations are O(log n); HashMap is O(1) average.

questions.questionText: What happens if you add a duplicate key to a HashMap?
options: The old value is replaced with the new value
questions.explanation: When a duplicate key is inserted into a HashMap, the old value associated with that key is replaced by the new value. The put() method returns the previous value.

questions.questionText: Which class provides a resizable-array implementation of the List interface?
questions.explanation: ArrayList implements List using a dynamically resizing internal array.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Iterator interface?
options: To traverse elements of a collection one by one
questions.hint: It has hasNext() and next() methods.
questions.explanation: Iterator provides a standard way to traverse any Collection element by element using hasNext() to check and next() to retrieve the next element.

options: Thrown when two threads access different collections
Thrown when a collection is modified while being iterated over (fail-fast)
Thrown when a collection exceeds its capacity
Thrown when null is added to a collection
questions.explanation: ConcurrentModificationException is thrown when a collection is structurally modified during iteration (e.g., adding/removing elements while iterating with a for-each loop).

questions.questionText: Which collection should you use if you need unique elements in sorted order?
questions.hint: It uses a tree structure to maintain order.
questions.explanation: TreeSet stores unique elements in sorted (natural or custom) order using a red-black tree internally.

options: Sorts a list in natural ascending order
questions.explanation: Collections.sort() sorts the specified List in ascending natural order (elements must implement Comparable).

questions.questionText: What is the load factor of a HashMap?
options: A threshold ratio that triggers resizing of the internal array
questions.explanation: The load factor (default 0.75) determines when a HashMap resizes. When the number of entries exceeds capacity * loadFactor, the internal array doubles in size and entries are rehashed.

questions.questionText: Which interface should a class implement to be used as a key in a HashMap?
options: It must override hashCode() and equals()
questions.hint: HashMap uses these two methods to locate and compare keys.
questions.explanation: For correct HashMap behavior, key objects must override both hashCode() (to determine bucket) and equals() (to handle collisions and key comparison).

questions.questionText: What is the difference between List and Set?
options: List allows duplicates and maintains insertion order; Set does not allow duplicates
Set is ordered; List is not
questions.hint: Think about uniqueness and ordering guarantees.
questions.explanation: List allows duplicate elements and maintains insertion order. Set does not allow duplicates (uniqueness enforced).

questions.questionText: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
options: Comparable defines natural ordering within the class; Comparator defines external ordering
Comparable is for primitives; Comparator is for objects
Comparable is deprecated in favor of Comparator
questions.hint: One uses compareTo(), the other uses compare().
questions.explanation: Comparable is implemented by the class itself (compareTo method) for natural ordering. Comparator is a separate class/lambda (compare method) for custom/alternative ordering.
